title: Lipid profile
subtitle: Total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides for cardiovascular risk assessment
summary: Lipid panel measurement for cardiovascular risk assessment and monitoring of statin therapy.
introduction: The lipid panel includes total cholesterol, LDL ('bad'), HDL ('good'), and triglycerides. Used to assess cardiovascular risk and guide preventive therapy. Fasting sample (12-hour) preferred for accurate triglyceride and LDL measurement.

rows.name: Total cholesterol
lowInterpretation: Total cholesterol <5.2 mmol/L: desirable cardiovascular risk profile. No statin therapy for primary prevention based on cholesterol alone.
highInterpretation: Total cholesterol 5.2–6.2 mmol/L: borderline; assess LDL and HDL. Lifestyle modification recommended.
Total cholesterol >6.2 mmol/L: elevated CVD risk. Check LDL (driver of risk), HDL, and triglycerides. Consider statin based on risk score.
notes: Crude marker; LDL more important for risk stratification.

rows.name: LDL cholesterol
rows.referenceRange: Optimal <1.8; Desirable <2.6; Borderline 2.6–3.4; High 3.4–4.1; Very high >4.1
lowInterpretation: LDL <1.8 mmol/L: very low CVD risk; optimal for high-risk patients or on statin therapy.
highInterpretation: LDL 2.6–3.4 mmol/L: borderline; lifestyle first-line; statin if high CVD risk.
LDL >3.4 mmol/L: elevated; statin therapy indicated based on CVD risk.
LDL >4.1 mmol/L: very high risk; high-dose statin (±ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor).
notes: Primary target for lipid-lowering therapy; more important than total cholesterol.
Calculated (Friedewald) when triglycerides <4.5 mmol/L; direct LDL when higher.

rows.name: HDL cholesterol
lowInterpretation: HDL <1.0 mmol/L (male) or <1.3 mmol/L (female): low protective cholesterol; increases CVD risk. Modifiable by exercise, weight loss, reduced alcohol.
highInterpretation: HDL >1.5 mmol/L: high protective cholesterol; cardiovascular protective effect. Associated with lower CVD risk.
notes: HDL is 'protective' cholesterol; higher is better.
Increases with exercise, weight loss, and moderate alcohol.
Strongest predictor of CVD outcome among lipids; low HDL + high LDL = very high risk.

rows.name: Triglycerides (fasting)
lowInterpretation: Triglycerides <1.7 mmol/L: normal; no increased CVD risk from hypertriglyceridaemia.
highInterpretation: Triglycerides 1.7–2.2 mmol/L: borderline; may reflect recent diet; repeat fasting sample.
Triglycerides 2.2–5.6 mmol/L: elevated; CVD risk factor. Manage with lifestyle (reduce refined carbs, alcohol, weight loss) and consider fibrate or omega-3.
Triglycerides >5.6 mmol/L: very high; risk of acute pancreatitis. Urgent treatment: fibrate, avoid alcohol, restrict fat <20 g/day.
notes: Fasting-dependent; non-fasting samples often falsely elevated.
Very high levels (>10 mmol/L) can cause pseudohyponatraemia; use direct LDL or apoB.
Triglycerides <1.0 mmol/L may reflect poor nutritional status; rarely requires treatment.

urgentFindings: Triglycerides >5.6 mmol/L (especially >10): risk of acute pancreatitis; urgent lifestyle intervention and consider fibrate.
LDL >4.1 mmol/L + established CVD or high-risk features: high-intensity statin (±additional agents) indicated.
Lipid abnormalities in acute illness: may be falsely low; repeat 6–8 weeks after acute event.
overrides: Do not start statin based on lipid levels alone; calculate absolute CVD risk using SCORE2 or Framingham.
In acute illness, lipid levels drop; repeat 6–8 weeks after resolution before treatment decisions.
Very high triglycerides (>10 mmol/L) make LDL calculation inaccurate; use direct LDL or apoB.

commonPatterns.title: Dyslipidaemia requiring treatment
interpretation: Lifestyle ± statin indicated based on absolute risk
actions: Start statin if high risk or established CVD

commonPatterns.title: Very high triglyceridaemia
findings: Family history of early MI or pancreatitis
actions: Genetic testing if very high (>10 mmol/L)

rationale: Hypothyroidism and liver disease worsen dyslipidaemia
If LDL >4.5 mmol/L in young patient
Strong family history of early CVD
